title: Oyster stitch
subtitle: A twisted chain and wrap that makes a small detached rosebud unit
excerpt: Oyster stitch produces a small, plump detached unit that resembles a tightly furled rosebud or a rounded petal. It begins with a twisted chain stitch, then a second pass wraps the thread around the base of the chain to swell and close the shape. Worked singly or in clusters, it is used for texture fills and floral details in surface embroidery.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), oyster stitch entry. Contemporary surface embroidery documentation of the twisted-chain-and-wrap construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A chain stitch variation where the needle enters beside rather than inside the previous loop, crossing the thread to produce a twisted, rope-like link.

content.text: Oyster stitch is a small detached unit built from a

loop with a wrapping thread that closes and swells its base. Each finished unit sits independently on the fabric like a small bud or seed. A cluster of oyster stitches worked close together fills a petal or leaf with a pleasingly uneven padded texture.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 to 3 strands, or perle 12; a round thread shows the twist clearly

content.text: Bring the thread up at point (A). This will be the base of the unit. Loop the working thread to the left and hold it down with your thumb.

Insert the needle at point (B), just to the right of (A) and slightly above it, crossing over the loop of thread. Bring the tip up at point (C), a short distance above (A) at the top of the planned unit. Pass the working thread under the needle tip from left to right to form a twisted chain. Pull through with gentle tension so the loop lies flat and the twist is visible.
Take the needle down at point (D), just below (C) and outside the tip of the loop, to hold the detached chain in place with a small securing stitch.

Bring the thread up again at (A), inside the base of the chain. Pass the needle and thread under the twisted base of the chain loop from right to left, without entering the fabric. Pull through and take the needle back down at (A) or very close to it. This wrap swells the base of the unit and gives the oyster its rounded shape.
Fasten off at the back, or bring the thread up at the starting point for the next unit. Each oyster stitch is worked individually.

items.symptom: The unit lies flat rather than plump
items.cause: The wrap at the base was not worked or was pulled too tight, collapsing the chain loop.
items.fix: Work the wrapping pass with relaxed tension. Slide the needle under the base threads and ease the loop gently outward before taking the thread down at (A).

items.symptom: The twisted chain has no visible twist
items.cause: The needle entered inside the previous thread loop rather than crossing over it.
items.fix: At step 2, make sure the needle goes down to the right of the thread and outside the loop, then comes up through the loop. The crossing at (B) creates the twist.

items.symptom: Units in a cluster look different sizes
items.cause: The distance between (A) and (C) varies from stitch to stitch.
items.fix: Mark a consistent stitch length with a chalk line or count threads before beginning a cluster fill.
